newsitem.title: USA: U.S. secondhand-smoke trial bedeviled by juror woes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. secondhand-smoke trial bedeviled by juror woes.

text.p: One of only two smokers on a six-member jury in the trial of a $5 billion secondhand-smoke case was dropped on Friday, the third juror or alternate to be excused since the panel was sworn in two days ago.

The dismissed juror, a female hospital-accounts worker, aged 43, was described by court staff as disruptive and a vocal complainer who might unfairly dominate the jury's deliberations on a verdict at the end of an estimated eight weeks of testimony scheduled to begin on Monday.

The trial judge, Robert Kaye of Dade County Circuit Court, ordered the juror replaced during a private meeting with lawyers on Friday, a court official said. The replacement juror, also a woman, is a non-smoking postal worker, aged 33.

The jury in the case -- Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris et al -- is now composed of two women and four men. Only one, a 30-year-old school counsellor, smokes. Two jurors are in their 50s, three in their 30s and one, a male cable-television installer, is 21.

The jury is to decide a landmark class-action suit brought on behalf of 60,000 flight attendants with tobacco-related illnesses such as lung cancer. All were non-smokers and claim their ailments were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke aboard U.S. passenger jets before 1988.
The case is the first secondhand-smoke case and the first class-action suit against the U.S. tobacco industry to come to trial.
On Thursday, after six weeks of painstaking individual questioning of potential jurors, Kaye excused two of 10 alternate jurors.
One, a business executive, said his work requires frequent travel to Latin America. A woman whose husband recently asked for a divorce cited personal difficulties.
Seven alternates remain, and no new alternates will be added, a court official said.
A trial consultant attending the court sessions said such a dropout rate among jurors so early in a trial was unusually high.
Opening statements are scheduled for Monday and plaintiff attorney Stanley Rosenblatt said he expected to start presenting his case on Wednesaday.
Rosenblatt said he expects to call as one of his first witnesses Julius Richmond, a U.S. surgeon general during the late 1970s under President Carter.
Rosenblatt told reporters he also expects to present on Wednesday videotaped questioning of James Morgan, chief executive of cigarette-maker Philip Morris Inc.
He declined to detail the questions Morgan answered in a deposition taken last April. The lawyer also said in court he intended to present videotaped depositions of other leading tobacco executives.
Kaye refused a request by Hugh Whiting, attorney for Reynolds Tobacco, that the Broin case's class-action status be ended and that each flight attendant sue individually.
